concept.name: Lambda Architecture (Batch + Stream)

relationships.description: Connects Lambda Architecture (Batch + Stream) to data warehousing lakehouse in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Lambda Architecture splits data processing into an immutable Batch Layer for exact historical truth and a low-latency Speed Layer for recent events, merging both in the Serving Layer.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use Lambda when you need sub-second approximate/recent views alongside deterministic, re-computable batch history—or choose Kappa (single stream replay) if your team cannot maintain two codebases.

concept.whyItMatters: Real-time analytics platforms (ad-tech billing, fraud dashboards, IoT telemetry) face a classic tension: streaming engines deliver <1s latency but struggle with late-arriving data, schema backfills, and complex global joins, while batch engines (Spark/Iceberg) guarantee exactness over petabytes at the cost of hours of latency. Lambda Architecture bridges both worlds—and understanding its dual-pipeline overhead explains why modern Lakehouse and Kappa designs evolved.
whenToUse: Systems requiring both sub-second operational visibility (Speed Layer) and auditable, bit-exact financial or regulatory reconciliation (Batch Layer).
Workloads with frequent late-arriving or out-of-order events (e.g., mobile SDKs offline for 48 hours) where batch reprocessing cleanly corrects prior stream approximations.
Legacy organizations that already have mature Spark/Snowflake batch pipelines and need to bolt on real-time Flink/Kafka views without rewriting historical ETL.
whenNotToUse: Small or mid-sized teams that cannot afford to write, test, and keep two separate codebases (e.g., Flink Java + Spark SQL) semantically identical—prefer Kappa Architecture instead.
Purely real-time operational alerting or stateful workflows where historical 5-year reprocessing is never needed.
Low-urgency BI reporting where 15–60 minute micro-batching (Spark Structured Streaming or Iceberg incremental loads) is fast enough.
keyPoints: Three-layer split: Immutable Master Dataset + Batch Layer (Spark/Iceberg) → Speed Layer (Flink/Kafka) → Serving Layer (ClickHouse/Druid/Cassandra) merging batch + real-time views at query time.
Immutability & recomputation: raw events are append-only in object storage (S3/GCS Parquet/Iceberg); any bug in transformation logic is fixed by re-running the Batch Layer over history.
Event-time watermarks vs. batch cutoffs: the Speed Layer tracks sliding windows via watermarks (e.g., 5-minute allowed lateness), while the Batch Layer sweeps everything older than T-1 hour.
Serving-layer merge: queries union precomputed batch views (`ts < cutoff`) with speed views (`ts >= cutoff`), or overwrite speed keys atomically when batch views finish.
Kappa alternative: retaining raw events in Kafka (or tiered storage) for 30+ days allows a single Flink job to handle both live traffic and historical replay, eliminating dual-codebase drift.

examples.title: Ad-Tech Click Attribution & Billing
examples.scenario: An ad network processes 400k clicks/sec; advertisers need live campaign pacing dashboards (<3s delay), while finance requires 100% deduplicated daily invoices.
examples.outcome: Kafka fans out clicks to Flink (updating Redis/Pinot real-time counters for pacing) and S3 Iceberg (hourly Spark deduplication + bot filtering that overwrites Pinot segments), achieving <2s dashboard freshness and zero billing discrepancies.

examples.title: E-Commerce Fraud & Velocity Scoring
examples.scenario: A checkout gateway computes 5-minute card velocity in real time while training 90-day historical merchant risk profiles.
examples.outcome: Flink computes 5-minute tumbling/sliding velocity in RocksDB state (<50 ms), while nightly Spark jobs recompute 90-day chargeback ratios into Cassandra, merged at inference time.

tradeOffs.factor: Lambda (Dual Batch + Speed) vs. Kappa (Stream-Only Replay)
tradeOffs.pro: Lambda leverages specialized batch engines (Spark/Trino) for massive petabyte joins and deterministic backfills without choking stream state.
tradeOffs.con: Maintaining two distinct implementations of business logic (e.g., Flink + Spark) inevitably causes subtle metric drift between live and historical numbers.

tradeOffs.factor: Query-Time Merge vs. Batch Overwrite in Serving Layer
tradeOffs.pro: Query-time union (`WHERE ts < cutoff` from batch + `ts >= cutoff` from speed) keeps batch writes non-blocking.
tradeOffs.con: Every dashboard query pays a 2x read fan-out and complex boundary deduplication; atomic segment replacement (Druid/Iceberg) simplifies reads.

tradeOffs.factor: Short Speed Retention vs. Long Kafka Replay Retention
tradeOffs.pro: Keeping only 2–6 hours in the Speed Layer bounds Flink RocksDB state size and memory cost.
tradeOffs.con: If the Batch Layer lags or fails for 8 hours, a 6-hour Speed Layer expires data before batch catches up, creating a blind spot.

failureModes.name: Semantic Logic Drift Between Batch and Speed
failureModes.description: A developer updates timezone handling or bot-filtering rules in the Spark batch job but forgets the Flink speed job, causing live metrics to jump or drop by 12% every hour when batch overwrites speed.
failureModes.mitigation: Share transformation logic via a single SQL/UDF library (e.g., Apache Beam, Spark Structured Streaming unified API, or dbt + Flink SQL) and run automated parity checks.

failureModes.name: Batch-Speed Boundary Gap or Double Counting
failureModes.description: Clock skew or delayed Kafka-to-S3 compaction causes events near the hourly cutoff to be either missed by both layers or counted twice.
failureModes.mitigation: Use deterministic event-time partition watermarks (`_ingest_cutoff_ts`) and idempotent upsert/segment replacement in the Serving Layer.

failureModes.name: Speed Layer Unbounded State Explosion
failureModes.description: A Flink `keyBy(userId)` aggregation without state TTL accumulates billions of keys over weeks, exhausting RocksDB disk and checkpointing timeouts.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce `StateTtlConfig` slightly longer than the maximum batch-recovery SLA (e.g., 24–48h) since older history lives in the Batch Layer.

failureModes.name: Small-File Explosion in Master Dataset
failureModes.description: Writing raw Kafka micro-batches to S3 every 60 seconds creates millions of 50 KB Parquet files, slowing Spark batch scans by 20x.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake with scheduled compaction (`rewrite_data_files`) to merge small files into 128–512 MB blocks.

commonMistakes: Implementing Lambda by default when a 1-minute micro-batch (Spark Structured Streaming) or a single Flink Kappa pipeline would satisfy the SLA.
Forgetting to retain raw immutable events in object storage, making it impossible to replay/fix historical bugs.
Using processing time (`System.currentTimeMillis()`) instead of event time in the Speed Layer, corrupting hourly boundaries during Kafka consumer lag.
Setting Speed Layer retention shorter than the Batch Layer's worst-case failure recovery time.
Storing mutable state directly in the Master Dataset instead of appending immutable event records.

sections.content:
## The idea

Proposed by Nathan Marz, **Lambda Architecture** solves the apparent conflict between low-latency streaming and fault-tolerant historical accuracy by splitting every incoming event into two parallel paths. The **Batch Layer** persists an immutable, append-only Master Dataset (e.g., S3 + Apache Iceberg) and periodically recomputes exact batch views from scratch or incremental partitions. Simultaneously, the **Speed Layer** (e.g., Apache Flink) processes only recent events in sub-second time. A **Serving Layer** (e.g., ClickHouse, Apache Druid, or Pinot) indexes both views so queries see immediate updates that are later replaced by authoritative batch truth.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace an e-commerce order event (`order_id: 7741`, `event_ts: 14:02:10Z`, `amount: $120`) through a Lambda pipeline:
1. **Ingest**: The checkout service publishes the event to Kafka topic `orders.raw` (7-day retention).
2. **Speed Path**: Apache Flink consumes `orders.raw`, updates a 1-hour tumbling revenue counter in RocksDB, and sinks to Redis/Pinot within **400 ms** so the live ops dashboard reflects `$120` immediately.
3. **Master Dataset**: Kafka Connect / Flink sinks raw events into S3 `s3://lake/orders_raw/` partitioned by `dt=2026-11-12/hr=14`.
4. **Batch Path**: At `15:10Z`, an hourly Spark job runs over `hr=14`, deduplicates retries, joins currency FX tables, and writes the authoritative view to Druid/ClickHouse, atomically replacing the `hr=14` speed-layer segment.

sections.content:
## Lambda vs. Kappa vs. Lakehouse

Modern data engineering has largely converged on two evolutions of Lambda:
- **Kappa Architecture**: Drops the Batch Layer entirely. Kafka (with tiered storage to S3) holds long-term history; when logic changes, you spin up a new Flink consumer group at offset 0 and swap the Serving Layer pointer once caught up.
- **Unified Lakehouse Streaming**: Engines like Apache Iceberg + Flink/Spark Structured Streaming write directly to one ACID table format, using incremental micro-batches (30–60s) when sub-second latency isn't strictly required.

## Architecture Pattern Comparison

| Architecture | Typical End-to-End Latency | Codebases to Maintain | Historical Backfill | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lambda** | <1s (Speed) + 1–24h (Batch) | 2 (Stream + Batch) | Re-run Spark over S3/Iceberg | High-scale billing + live ops dashboards |
| **Kappa** | <1s | 1 (Stream only) | Replay Kafka tiered storage | Teams wanting single-pipeline simplicity |
| **Lakehouse Micro-Batch** | 30s–5m | 1 (Unified SQL/Spark) | Time-travel / `MERGE INTO` | BI, ML features, general analytics |
| **Pure Batch** | 1–24h | 1 (Batch only) | Full or partition overwrite | Financial close, daily reporting |

## Failure modes

1. **Dual-Codebase Divergence**: Subtle differences in null handling, late-event windows, or floating-point rounding between Flink and Spark cause visible metric jumps at every batch handoff.
2. **Handoff Double-Counting**: Overlapping time windows between the Speed Layer and Batch Layer inflate totals unless the Serving Layer uses deterministic partition replacement or idempotent keys.
3. **Checkpoint / Compaction Bottlenecks**: Unbounded state in Flink or uncompacted tiny Parquet files in S3 degrade both layers simultaneously.

## Boundary Synchronization & Parity Testing

To prevent boundary gaps, partition both layers by **event time** (`event_ts` truncated to hour) rather than ingestion time, and have the Serving Layer route queries cleanly via a watermark table (`last_verified_batch_hour`). Run an automated daily parity diff comparing the Speed Layer's pre-overwrite hour against the Batch Layer's output; alert if divergence exceeds 0.5%.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Confirm you genuinely need <5s latency AND petabyte batch recomputation before choosing Lambda over Kappa or micro-batch.
- [ ] Persist raw events immutably in Parquet/Iceberg with scheduled small-file compaction.
- [ ] Align both Batch and Speed layers on event-time boundaries, not wall-clock processing time.
- [ ] Set Speed Layer state TTLs > 2x your worst-case Batch Layer recovery window.
- [ ] Automate hourly parity checks between Speed and Batch outputs to catch logic drift early.

interviewProblems.title: Lambda Architecture (Batch + Stream)
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Lambda Architecture (Batch + Stream). What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Lambda Architecture splits data processing into an immutable Batch Layer for exact historical truth and a low-latency Speed Layer for recent events, merging both in the Serving Layer.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Speed Layer applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Serving Layer.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Serving Layer experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Share transformation logic via a single SQL/UDF library (e.g., Apache Beam, Spark Structured Streaming unified API, or dbt + Flink SQL) and run automated parity checks.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use Lambda when you need sub-second approximate/recent views alongside deterministic, re-computable batch history—or choose Kappa (single stream replay) if your team cannot maintain two codebases.
Avoid trap: Implementing Lambda by default when a 1-minute micro-batch (Spark Structured Streaming) or a single Flink Kappa pipeline would satisfy the SLA.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to retain raw immutable events in object storage, making it impossible to replay/fix historical bugs.
When to reach for it: Systems requiring both sub-second operational visibility (Speed Layer) and auditable, bit-exact financial or regulatory reconciliation (Batch Layer).
When to reach for it: Workloads with frequent late-arriving or out-of-order events (e.g., mobile SDKs offline for 48 hours) where batch reprocessing cleanly corrects prior stream approximations.

putItTogether.title: Putting Lambda Batch Stream Together
putItTogether.summary: Use Lambda when you need sub-second approximate/recent views alongside deterministic, re-computable batch history—or choose Kappa (single stream replay) if your team cannot maintain two codebases.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Lambda Batch Stream before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Kafka fans out clicks to Flink (updating Redis/Pinot real-time counters for pacing) and S3 Iceberg (hourly Spark deduplication + bot filtering that overwrites Pinot segments), achieving <2s dashboard freshness and zero billing discrepancies.
